| Traffic type | Matches rule | Action | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| AD ports you list in the allow rule (e.g. TCP 389/636/3268 …, UDP 88/123 …) | **Priority 100** allow | **Allowed** | Highest-priority match permits it |
| Any other outbound traffic | Skips priority 100 (ports don't match) → hits **priority 1000** deny | **Blocked** | Deny overrides the implied allow |
| Anything not caught by the explicit rules | Implied allow-egress rule (priority 65535) | **Ignored** | Lower priority, so never reached |

[![](https://img-c.udemycdn.com/redactor/raw/practice_test_question_explanation/2025-05-14_14-43-40-1cff14f5558d076e8e08d6e3df22d8e5.JPG)

| Option | What happens | Why it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **B**: deny 100, allow 1000 | Traffic hits the **deny (priority 100)** first and is blocked before it reaches the lower-priority allow rule. | Lower number → higher priority. |
| **C**: allow 1000 only, rely on an "implied deny 100" | There is **no implied deny-egress rule**. The implied rule is *allow*, so all other traffic stays open. | The implied egress rule is allow (priority 65535), not deny. |
| **D**: allow 100 only, rely on an "implied deny 1000" | Again, no implied deny-egress rule exists. Traffic that doesn't match the allow rule falls through to the implied **allow-egress**, so nothing is blocked. | Same as C. |

    # ... login logic ...

    session = datastore_client.get(session_key)

5-26.explanation:
**Correct answer: C**

**Move the HQ self-managed MySQL database to Cloud SQL. Standardize the database schema across all plants, and configure each plant's database as an external read replica for Cloud SQL.**

**Why C is correct**

- Only HQ writes the data, and every plant needs an exact, read-only copy. That is primary/replica replication.
- Cloud SQL for MySQL supports **external replicas**: MySQL servers outside Google Cloud (here, at each plant) that replicate from a Cloud SQL primary. See https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/configure-external-replica.
- MySQL replication applies every committed change in order, and replica status (lag, errors) shows whether a plant is in sync. That is the "simple way to confirm" HQ wants, and it removes the XML export, FTP and parsing steps that caused the drift.
- Replication needs compatible schemas and versions, which is why the option standardizes the plant schemas first. The case study's schema drift is the problem to fix, not a constraint to keep.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- **A / B. Pub/Sub topics per supplier.** You would have to build your own change capture, ordering, retries and reconciliation at each plant. It replaces one custom sync process with another and gives no built-in way to prove a plant matches HQ.
- **D. Database Migration Service continuous migration to the plants.** Database Migration Service migrates *into* Google Cloud: its destinations are Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, not on-premises MySQL servers (https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview). It cannot replicate from Cloud SQL out to the plant databases, and it is a migration tool, not a permanent multi-site distribution mechanism.
5-26.why: Database Migration Service only supports Cloud SQL and AlloyDB as destinations, so D (replicating from Cloud SQL to on-premises plant databases) is not possible. Cloud SQL for MySQL documents external replicas for exactly this one-writer, many-readers pattern, and option C standardizes the schema that replication requires.
